item.title: ‘The Shack’ author expects more Christian criticism with sequel, but will take it in stride
item.description: William P. Young suggets his sequel "Return to the Shack" will again draw pushback from Christians who hold what he calls a fear-based religion.
item.content:encoded:
Some Christians dismissed author William P. Young’s novel "The Shack" as heresy for its portrayal of the Holy Trinity, and he said he expects more pushback on his sequel.

"The Shack," which was also adapted into a major motion picture in 2017, tells the heartbreaking story of a father, Mack, whose daughter is kidnapped and killed while on a camping trip. In the midst of his grief, Mack discovers a letter in his mailbox from God, who implores him to visit a shack. Once there, he meets a diverse Holy Trinity. Papa is a middle-aged Black woman, Jesus is a Middle Eastern carpenter, and the Holy Spirit is an Asian woman named Sarayu. 

Some Christians balked at the unorthodox portrayals, saying Young sorely misrepresented the nature of God. America magazine's David E. Nantais wrote at the time that the book had become "both a fascination and an object of contempt to millions of Christians" because it literally portrayed the Trinity as three persons.

Young's sequel, "Return to the Shack: A Journey into Redemption," is out on bookshelves in October. And he expects Christians to again make some noise because of the subject matter.

AT PENTECOST, THE HOLY SPIRIT MANIFESTS IN EACH BELIEVER IN A 'RADICALLY UNIQUE WAY,' SAYS FAITH LEADER

"You know, I don't brace for any of it," Young told Fox News Digital. "Yes, it'll probably happen. But yes, if you're going to have something out in public purview, you'll always find people who don't like it. And that's fine with me. I think — and I did get considerable but not overwhelming pushback from my own people — because of my history as a missionary kid, a preacher's kid."

An additional aspect of his new novel that may raise eyebrows is how the child murderer, simply named J, is portrayed. J is now a death row inmate, and Young gives him a more humanized storyline in the sequel, including references to his childhood and abusive father. Young said he decided to go that route because of what he experienced through his own broken relationship with his dad.

In candid interviews since "The Shack" was released, Young has described his father as angry, distant, and strict. His novel helped him repair their relationship and show mercy toward his father.

"He was allowed only to be a failed father," Young told Fox News Digital. "And so I finally released him from my expectations and allowed him to become something greater than a failure to my expectations and greater than being my dad. And that was to finally become a human being. And when that happened, suddenly his story mattered."

Young shared that some of the prisoners in the sequel are modeled after death row inmates he befriended at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, so he felt compelled to view them through a sympathetic lens, too.

"That's just one of the layers that's going on," Young said. "But I think that death row inmates would be one of the most related to as animals, put into category. Like the guys say, 'We're only known for the worst day of our lives.'"

JD VANCE REVEALS WHAT DREW HIM BACK TO GOD AFTER SEEING CHRISTIANS HAD LIFE ‘FIGURED OUT’

LOST PAGES WITH 'GHOST' TEXT RECOVERED FROM ONE OF THE WORLD'S MOST IMPORTANT NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS

"We're talking about human beings who've come from very diverse backgrounds and situations and trauma being a very centerpiece, abuse being a centerpiece," he added.

Young says, however, that people should not use that as an excuse for the choices they make. He surmised that some of the Christians who took issue with his first book have "a fear-based religion."

"And there is no fear in love, that's a Scripture out of the New Testament," he said. "So any degree of fear, that's in your sense of the transcendent, in your sense of the higher power, your sense of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Any fear indicates that your theology, your religion is seriously flawed. And because people are afraid, they're going to react out of their fear."

‘RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST’ WRITER REVEALS MEL GIBSON'S DARK SPIRITUAL WARNING ABOUT ‘PASSION’ FOLLOW-UP

Young sympathized with some of the reaction, however. Over the years, he's admitted to marital infidelity and how that impacted his own walk with God.

"If it hadn't been for that kind of monumental failure — when you get caught you have to either run or face it. I think it's by the grace of God that I faced it," Young told Oregon Live in 2015.

"And I get that, because I've been there and done that," he told Fox News Digital. "You know, I went through enough crap and did enough harm and had to deal with the consequences of that in my own life, that I know who I am now. And I'm not a book, and I'm not a movie. That's not my identity." 

"My identity is outside of that," Young continued. "And so, you know, sometimes I think if people are bothered by something, it means something is in them that needs to be addressed and it becomes an invitation. And I'm excited for that to happen in people's lives. If I can walk on the holy ground of their story a little bit, I'm honored."

Young said he "absolutely" believes in miracles, like Mack receiving a letter from God.

"I absolutely believe something like that could happen," he said. "Like I've said, I've never heard God speak audibly, but I believe that God is in union with every single person who's ever been conceived. And God is not mute, but God is not coercive. And if you want to see what the character and nature of God is like, look at Jesus, read the Gospel, read John or one of the Gospels, and you'll see how love lives in this world."

"So I'm one of those who is — I don't like a purpose-driven life — I like a spirit-indwelt, moment-by-moment participatory life," he continued. "And I'm good with that."

item.title: Gen Keane questions whether Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar can be trusted in Iran talks
item.description: Retired Gen. Jack Keane accuses Pakistan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia of being compromised mediators who steer Trump away from military pressure on Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Retired Army Gen. Jack Keane questioned whether Pakistan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia can be trusted to help shape negotiations with Iran, accusing the regional partners of steering President Donald Trump away from military pressure while leaving the United States and Israel to bear the risks of confronting Tehran.

Keane, a Fox News senior strategic analyst and former Army vice chief of staff, said during a Monday appearance on Fox News’ "America’s Newsroom" that Pakistan and Qatar were "compromised" as mediators because, in his view, they favor Iran over the United States.

"It is well known in the Middle East region, by our intelligence services, by all the players, that the Pakistanis and the Qataris are compromised because they favor Iran at the expense of the United States," Keane said. "This is historical. This is not new."

NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT

Keane’s criticism contrasts with Trump’s public praise for Islamabad.

Trump said April 26 during a phone interview with Fox News that he had "great respect for Pakistan" because its officials had "been terrific" and "really tried" to advance negotiations with Iran. He added that Pakistan would remain involved in the process.

While speaking to reporters after the G7 summit in France on June 18, Trump also credited Pakistan and Qatar with helping advance the negotiations that produced the U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly also defended the administration’s regional partners, telling Fox News Digital that, "President Trump has great relationships with leaders from Pakistan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, and he appreciates the involvement of all of our regional partners who are assisting with negotiations." 

"If Iran cannot agree to a good deal with the United States, the fault will lie squarely with the regime, who will suffer the consequences," Kelly added.

Mediators were preparing a second memorandum focused exclusively on the Strait of Hormuz, Wednesday reports indicated, potentially separating the immediate maritime crisis from the broader dispute over Iran’s nuclear activities.

Keane, a former four-star general, argued that their involvement may have contributed to Washington misunderstanding Iran’s intentions.

"And yet they’re mediators," Keane said. "So their influence here, I think, had played a part in misleading the United States in terms of Iran’s real intentions."

TRUMP SAYS SAUDI NUCLEAR AGREEMENT WON'T MOVE FORWARD WITHOUT ABRAHAM ACCORDS: 'THEY HAVE TO BE A MEMBER'

Pakistan and Qatar have played formal roles in the diplomatic process.

A June 22 joint statement from the two countries said they were mediating talks between the United States and Iran under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. The framework established working groups on nuclear issues, sanctions, monitoring and dispute resolution, as well as a mechanism intended to prevent incidents involving commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pakistan declined to comment on Keane’s criticism. The Saudi and Qatari embassies in Washington did not respond by the time of publication.

Raza Rumi, editor-at-large of Pakistan’s The Friday Times, disputed Keane’s characterization, arguing that Islamabad’s working relationship with Tehran does not make it a compromised mediator.

IS THIS TRUMP’S LAST ‘LAST CHANCE’? CEASELESS STRING OF BROKEN CEASEFIRES FUELS DOUBT OVER IRAN DEAL

"Successful mediators are often those that enjoy channels of communication with all sides," Rumi told Fox News Digital, saying Pakistan’s approach is shaped more by geography, security and economic concerns than ideological alignment with Iran.

He noted that Pakistan shares a long border with Iran and wants to prevent further instability, while also maintaining longstanding ties with the United States and close partnerships with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Rumi also pointed to the exchange of strikes between Pakistan and Iran in January 2024 as evidence that relations between the neighbors are not uniformly close.

"The suggestion that Pakistan somehow caused Washington to misunderstand Tehran’s intentions is difficult to substantiate," Rumi said. "It would be a considerable stretch to attribute any American misreading of Iran’s intentions to Pakistani mediation."

Keane directed even sharper criticism at Saudi Arabia, saying that Riyadh denied the United States access to Saudi airspace and a U.S. air base during preparations for a possible operation to forcibly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also claimed Saudi officials had repeatedly persuaded Trump not to resume major military operations against Iran.

"The fact of the matter is, the Saudis are not willing to sacrifice to rid the Middle East region of Iran’s aggression," Keane said, describing the potential costs as casualties and damage to Saudi oil infrastructure.

"They’re willing for us to make that sacrifice, for sure," he added. "They’re willing for Israel to make that sacrifice, for sure."

His remarks highlighted a broader debate over whether Saudi caution represents an unwillingness to confront Tehran or a strategic effort to prevent an open-ended regional war.

GULF COUNTRIES STRONGLY CONDEMN IRAN'S DRONE ATTACK ON BAHRAIN AS RISING TENSIONS THREATEN MOU

Salman Al-Ansari, a Saudi geopolitical analyst, rejected the suggestion that Riyadh is unwilling to confront Iran, saying the Kingdom distinguishes between credible deterrence and military action without clear objectives.

"Saudi Arabia supports confronting Iranian aggression, but not an open-ended regional war without clear objectives or an endgame," Al-Ansari told Fox News Digital.

"Riyadh favors diplomacy backed by credible deterrence, but any agreement must be enforceable and verifiable, addressing Iran’s nuclear program, its proxies, and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," he added.

A Gulf affairs analyst who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue offered a different assessment, saying Saudi leaders fear that a wider confrontation would expose the Kingdom’s critical infrastructure to Iranian retaliation.

"Saudi Arabia believes it should appease Iran because it is deeply concerned about the consequences of a broader confrontation," the analyst said. "Riyadh fears the damage Iran could inflict on the Kingdom’s infrastructure and has therefore favored restraint and negotiations over a decisive military campaign."

The analyst described a widening divide among Gulf states, arguing that Saudi Arabia and Qatar favor accommodation while the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait support stronger pressure on Iran.

Richard Goldberg, a senior adviser at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank and former National Security Council official, said during a separate Fox News appearance Wednesday, that Washington continues to depend on Saudi infrastructure even as disagreements persist over military strategy.

"When we talk about the Gulf states, we talk about Saudi Arabia and General Keane’s comments, remember, we also are relying on Saudi Arabia with their overland pipelines to keep us in the game here," Goldberg said. "The fact that they’re at maximum capacity moving through the Red Sea also allows us to continue the strangulation strategy."

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

The debate comes as the United States and Iran continue negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz.

Oman, Pakistan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia all have been involved in the diplomatic effort, while reports Wednesday indicated that mediators were working on an interim arrangement that could establish separate shipping routes through Iranian and Omani waters as broader nuclear negotiations continue.

The central question is whether those negotiations can produce an enforceable agreement or merely allow Tehran to preserve its leverage over the waterway.

Keane said he remained doubtful that Iran was prepared to surrender meaningful control.

"They are not going to give up the Strait of Hormuz," he said. "They think it’s a strategic asset."

He predicted Iran would seek to retain some degree of control over the waterway and warned that reaching an agreement on Iran’s nuclear program would be even more difficult.

"My gut feeling here is no," Keane said when asked whether Iran was prepared to reach and implement a substantive agreement. "The president is not going to make a bad deal here."

item.title: Senate moves to unshackle America's drivers from California's 'climate zealots'
item.description: Senate Republicans target EPA waivers under the Clean Air Act that gave California authority over vehicle emissions and gas-powered lawn equipment.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Senate Republicans are launching a multi-front effort targeting the legal framework they say allows California to exert outsized influence over vehicle and equipment emissions standards beyond its borders, creating economic and consumer consequences.

Republicans argue California has become the nation's de facto emissions regulator — as manufacturers rarely create separate product lines for the Golden State and instead are inclined to build to California’s standards, creating implicit national requirements.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo. — a top member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (EPW) — is leading the effort alongside Sens. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., Jon Husted, R-Ohio, and Pete Ricketts, R-Neb. They argue EPA waivers granted to California during the Obama and Biden administrations under the Clean Air Act have turned narrow environmental exceptions into de facto climate regulation, advancing the state's sweeping climate agenda.

"California's climate zealots have run roughshod over the rest of the country for too long," Lummis told Fox News Digital.

CALIFORNIA SUES TRUMP EPA OVER MOVE TO SUBJECT STATE VEHICLE EMISSIONS WAIVERS TO CONGRESSIONAL REVIEW

"Under Governor Newsom, Sacramento has decided it can dictate what Wyoming families drive and what equipment our small businesses use. That ends today."

Last year, lawmakers successfully rescinded three Biden-era EPA waivers allowing California to create emissions standards for trucks, cars and buses that they said gave the state outsized regulatory control. Thursday’s package goes a step further by targeting earlier EPA decisions they say laid the legal foundation for those now-rescinded regulations.

Each resolution uses the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to nullify a different EPA waiver. The CRA gives Congress the power to check agencies' executive power.

NEWSOM, WALZ URGE CONGRESS TO BLOCK ANTI-CLIMATE BILL IN THEIR ‘WOKE’ CRUSADE

Because the CRA bars agencies from issuing rules that are "substantially the same" without new authorization from Congress, Republicans argue overturning the waivers would prevent future administrations from simply reinstating them — which targets the legal foundation of such carveouts.

Collectively, the package targets California's authority over gas-powered lawn equipment, passenger vehicle emissions standards, the Advanced Clean Cars program and the original 2009 EPA waiver allowing Sacramento to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from automobiles.

In the 1960s, the Clean Air Act gave California a narrow carve-out to seek EPA waivers for emissions rules that could be stricter than federal standards — but critics say the exemption, originally intended to address severe Los Angeles smog, has been weaponized to force manufacturing changes that reverberate across the country.

Andrew Bray, an executive with the National Association of Landscape Professionals, whose members rely on small off-road engines affected by the waivers, said he supports a responsible transition to lower-emission equipment — but underlined that it must come from "practical innovation" and not government mandates.

TRUMP’S REINDUSTRIALIZATION AGENDA FACES ITS BIGGEST HURDLE — AMERICANS

"This resolution is a critical step in securing the flexibility businesses need while technology continues to advance," Bray said. Michael Lee of the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America added that the legislative process, not state-specific fiats with "nationwide consequences," is the way to address the situation.

The four lawmakers leading the fight said in a release that California regulators have "abandoned any pretense of addressing local air quality and turned the waiver process into a backdoor for imposing a radical climate agenda on the entire country… without a single vote in Congress."

Lummis' resolution would rescind a 2025 waiver granted just before President Donald Trump took office that she said allowed California to phase out gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws and leaf blowers.

In doing so, manufacturers would no longer be inclined to transition to electric or zero-emission models.

TRUMP'S EPA CHIEF PUSHES BACK ON CLIMATE SKEPTICS BEING LABELED 'SCIENCE DENIERS'

Lummis' resolution targets a 2025 EPA waiver that allowed California to move toward phasing out new gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws, leaf blowers and lawn mowers. Supporters say repealing the waiver would remove regulatory pressure encouraging manufacturers to transition those products toward zero-emission technology.

Husted’s resolution targets a 2022 EPA waiver that restored California’s authority to continue its Advanced Clean Cars program.

"Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to follow California’s lead when it comes to policies that make everyday life more expensive and less convenient," he told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

Ricketts said the situation is proof that the Obama-Biden era of "overregulation and red tape" continues to cost Nebraskans and Americans writ large millions of dollars, citing his state's massive agricultural industry as an example of regulatory reverberations from Sacramento.

EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

"They used California policies as a backdoor EV mandate and even tried to control how we cut our grass," he said. His CRA resolution targets an Obama-era waiver originally authorizing the clean car program, while Schmitt seeks repeal of a waiver granted just months after President George W. Bush left office that allows California to enforce greenhouse gas emissions standards for new passenger vehicles beginning with the 2009 model year.

Schmitt said the waivers allow Sacramento to "continue to punish" manufacturers around the country and affect consumer choice and costs through their "climate alarmist rules."

Together, Republicans say the four resolutions represent Congress' broadest effort yet to unshackle states and manufacturers from California's emissions framework by targeting not only individual regulations but the EPA decisions they argue made those regulations possible.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Opponents are expected to counter that the effort would undermine California's longstanding authority under the Clean Air Act to adopt stricter environmental standards.

Fox News Digital reached out to former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, as well as California Gov. Gavin Newsom, for comment.

item.title: Popular smoothie ingredient may reduce one key health benefit, study suggests
item.description: A viral video claims bananas degrade blueberry benefits in smoothies, based on recent research, but dietitians argue that fruit shouldn't be villainized.
item.content:encoded:
Bananas are a smoothie staple, but a viral social media video has raised questions about whether they could reduce the nutritional benefits of other ingredients, such as blueberries.

In a July appearance on the "Mel Robbins Podcast," Dr. Rhonda Patrick, a biomedical scientist and founder of FoundMyFitness, demonstrated how she likes to make her smoothies, which do not include bananas.

Bananas contain polyphenol oxidase (PPO), an enzyme that can break down polyphenols, which are beneficial for gut, heart and brain health, according to Patrick, who is based in San Diego. PPO is also responsible for turning cut fruit brown.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

Recent studies suggest that when a banana is added to a blueberry smoothie, fewer beneficial polyphenols are absorbed from the berries.

Instead, Patrick uses avocado to give the smoothie the same creamy texture with 95% less sugar, she said. Avocado also adds more vitamins and monounsaturated fat, which can increase absorption of carotenoids, like lutein and zeaxanthin, from kale in the smoothie.

This opinion sparked debate in the online nutrition community, with some dietitians and nutritionists arguing that bananas should not be villainized based on a small body of research.

STUDY FINDS SPECIAL TOMATO DRINK MAY REDUCE INFLAMMATION IN ADULTS WITH OBESITY

The study Patrick referenced, which was published in the journal Food & Function in 2023, analyzed food absorption in eight healthy men.

On separate days, participants drank either a banana smoothie (high in an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase), drank a mixed berry smoothie (low in the enzyme) or took flavan-3-ol capsules (dietary supplements that contain concentrated plant compounds) with milk.

Blood tests showed that people absorbed about 84% fewer beneficial plant compounds after drinking the banana smoothie than after taking the flavan-3-ol capsules.

While researchers didn't test a banana-blueberry smoothie, the results suggest that bananas could reduce the benefits of foods high in flavan-3-ols.

LIVING LONGER COULD HINGE ON SURPRISING DIETARY CHANGE, STUDY REVIEW SUGGESTS

Los Angeles-based registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein, author of the upcoming book "Beyond the Shot," said the findings are "interesting," but don't tell the whole story.

"It doesn't mean the smoothie loses all of its health benefits," she said. "You're still getting fiber from the banana, and many other beneficial nutrients from polyphenol-rich fruits."

Muhlstein pointed out that the study included only eight participants and has not yet been replicated. She also noted that researchers used a standardized cocoa-derived flavanol supplement instead of whole fruits, such as berries, which may be absorbed differently by the body.

In a follow-up post on Instagram, responding to the backlash from the original post, Patrick said, "You can add bananas to your blueberry smoothies. However, you should know that you are going to degrade some of the polyphenols in those blueberries."

"Bananas are nutritious, I eat them, and this is not a reason to stop," she added in the caption. "But if your goal is to preserve as many of the berry polyphenols as possible, the chemistry matters."

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

Not every beneficial compound in blueberries will be eliminated by bananas, Patrick wrote, as the fruit contains many other polyphenols, including anthocyanins.

"This was a small study that should be replicated," she said. "But the magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie."

New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco agreed that the findings don't mean everyone should avoid bananas.

Unlike well-established advice to limit processed meats and added sugar, the guidance on bananas is more nuanced and doesn't apply to everyone, she told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

As nutrition advice spreads on social media, DeCicco said it's important to remember that everyone's health needs are different and to consult a doctor before following online recommendations.

The broader issue, she noted, is that Americans aren’t eating enough nutrient-rich foods, like bananas and berries, and are instead consuming more processed foods that have been linked to chronic disease.

"That’s why Americans are fatter and sicker than they've ever been, so I think focus on that more," DeCicco advised. "It doesn't need to be so complicated all the time … If you're eating a banana instead of french fries, that's good."

Nutrition should be individualized, DeCicco said. Someone who eats mostly fast-food should focus on replacing processed foods with fruits and vegetables, while someone with a more advanced nutrition plan may benefit from limiting high-carb, high-sugar fruits like bananas.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For those trying to lose weight and balance blood sugar, choosing fruits that are lower in sugar and higher in fiber may help with these outcomes.

"It really [depends] on where you're coming from and what your health journey is," DeCicco said.

Those looking to maximize polyphenol intake can swap bananas for frozen zucchini, avocado or Greek yogurt in smoothies for the same creamy texture, Muhlstein added.

FIRST ON FOX: An illegal immigrant’s alleged hit-and-run that critically injured an elderly woman outside her Miami-Dade home prompted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to urge local authorities to "cooperate with us and not release this criminal from jail."

Seventy-four-year-old Geraldine Byrd, who neighbors described as "kind" and friendly, is on life support in critical condition after authorities say she was run over by illegal immigrant Tomas Raymundo Brito, according to CBS Miami.

The outlet reported that Brito allegedly struck Byrd twice outside her home early Sunday morning. Byrd had stepped out of her car to open her gate when Brito allegedly struck her vehicle, causing it to spin into Byrd before his truck allegedly struck her again, trapping her underneath the vehicle.

Neighbors were reportedly alerted to the crash by the sound of a loud boom. One neighbor, Kristina Diaz, told NBC 6 South Florida that "we could hear screaming, we could hear everybody yelling, ‘Where is she? Oh, she’s underneath the car. Call 911.’"

MAN CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED MOTHER AND TWO YOUNG SONS HAS ICE DETAINER, PRIOR DWI CONVICTIONS

The same neighbor told the outlet that Byrd "would always send my daughter gifts for her birthday. So, she was a very kind woman." Speaking in Spanish, another neighbor, Flor Ortiz, told CBS Miami that she and Byrd "do not speak the same language, but we always greet each other. She is a good person."

After the incident, Brito allegedly got out of the truck and fled the scene. A family member of Byrd’s reportedly chased him down and found him hiding in a shed. After his arrest, Brito reportedly admitted he was the driver and said he drank five beers before the incident.

Byrd was airlifted to a nearby hospital and remains on life support in critical condition, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

Brito was charged with leaving the scene of a crash causing serious bodily injury and driving without a license.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF TRYING TO DISARM VIRGINIA POLICE OFFICER

Fox News Digital learned that ICE lodged a detainer with the Miami-Dade Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center the same day Brito was arrested.

Brito entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location, according to DHS. He is a Guatemalan national.

"This criminal illegal alien from Guatemala is charged with hit-and-run after a drunk-driving accident that sent a 74-year-old woman to the hospital in critical condition in Miami-Dade County," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"He should have never been allowed in our communities or on our streets," Mullin continued, adding, "ICE is asking officials in Miami-Dade County to cooperate with us and not release this criminal from jail, and to turn him over to ICE custody so we can remove him from our country."

Mullin added that "thanks to the strong leadership of President Donald Trump, ICE is unleashed to go after criminal illegal aliens like this one so that we can make America safe again."

A spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Corrections and Rehabilitation Department confirmed with Fox News Digital that the department had received ICE's request and that Brito is currently in custody.

The spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "Miami-Dade County honors these detainer requests in accordance with the law by holding the individual for the authorized 48-hour period."

The spokesperson said that "if ICE does not take custody of the individual within that timeframe, the individual is released as required by law."

"Miami-Dade County and the Miami-Dade Corrections and Rehabilitation Department comply with all applicable laws regarding immigration detainer requests and do not deny detainer requests submitted by federal authorities," the spokesperson added.

NEW MAINE LAW LIMITS POLICE COOPERATION WITH FEDERAL IMMIGRATION OFFICIALS

Miami-Dade County is not a sanctuary jurisdiction, and Florida law prohibits sanctuary policies. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office also participates in ICE's 287(g) program under state law.

She added that "immigrants helped build Miami-Dade County, and our community has always believed that public safety, the rule of law, and respect for human dignity can go hand in hand."

item.title: Rand Paul predicts Fauci contempt vote will pass, vows swift DOJ referral
item.description: Rand Paul says the votes are there to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after the former NIAID director invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans are readying immediate ramifications for Dr. Anthony Fauci's refusal to testify last week in the upper chamber, and the leader of the push believes the votes are there to pull it off.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and his Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs are slated to decide whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress for declining to answer lawmakers’ questions after being subpoenaed to testify, and, instead, invoking the Fifth Amendment on Thursday morning.

"I think there is a very good chance that we will win the vote," Paul told Fox News Digital.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

And if successful, Paul wants to get the Department of Justice (DOJ) involved swiftly.

"The next step will be when we send the referral over directly to the Department of Justice," he said.

Paul unveiled the contempt resolution on Tuesday, which stipulated that once reported from committee, it would be sent to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia.

The Kentucky Republican has spent years challenging Fauci, who previously served as the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) director and played a major role in the country’s policy and messaging on COVID-19 during the pandemic.

WATCH: RAND PAUL SAYS THERE'S ONE THING AMERICANS HAVE NEVER HEARD FROM FAUCI

He’s charged that Fauci should be thrown in prison and sought to compel him to admit that the virus sprang from a lab leak in Wuhan, China, in connection to risky research allegedly funded under his direction.

Last week’s hearing was meant to be the ultimate battle between the two and the pinnacle of Paul’s yearslong crusade against Fauci. But that didn’t happen when Fauci, under advice from his lawyers, pleaded the Fifth Amendment well over 100 times during the hearing.

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Those became the last words that the former chief medical advisor to the president uttered in the hearing beyond invoking his constitutional rights.

That prompted Paul to tee up a vote on contempt charges against him in a bid to compel Fauci to speak. The lawmaker also cast doubt on whether Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth Amendment comported with his sweeping pardon from former President Joe Biden on his way out of office.

Biden granted Fauci a full and unconditional pardon for all actions taken between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025.

"I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon, and that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity," Paul said as the hearing closed.

When asked to expand on the legal question looming over Fauci’s pardon, Paul declined. "It’s a good legal discussion, and we will make those legal points to DOJ in sending the referral over," Paul said.

item.title: STEVE MOORE: The IRS became judge, jury and executioner in a tax-code witch hunt against Americans
item.description: An aggressive IRS enforcement campaign has swept more than 1,100 syndicated conservation-easement disputes into audits and litigation.
item.content:encoded:
I’m a flat tax guy like Steve Forbes, chairman and editor-in-chief, Forbes Media and author of "Flat Tax Revolution," so in an ideal world, we wouldn’t stuff the IRS tax code with special tax breaks and instead would have one simple, low rate of 18% for everyone.

But if Congress passes tax laws steering people and businesses into certain activities, it can’t just snatch those incentives away indiscriminately. This is called a "bait-and-switch" trap, and here’s a perfect example of such a misdeed.

More than 60 years ago, the IRS created a program called a conservation easement through a revenue ruling. Its goal was to protect nature, stop development, and save working lands. Landowners received a tax incentive for voluntarily setting aside a portion of their land from development. The law has been in effect since 1976 — nearly 50 years. The tax break was made permanent in 1980 and has been part of the tax code ever since.

To further encourage this land preservation policy, individuals, business partnerships and corporations were permitted to donate to these land easements in exchange for a tax write-off. The result? Tens of millions of acres have been conserved.

IRS RAISES BUSINESS MILEAGE DEDUCTION RATE AMID FUEL PRICE SURGE

Then, in late 2016, IRS officials who disapproved of these syndicated conservation-easement transactions unilaterally changed the rules of the game. Notice 2017-10 did not formally abolish the conservation-easement deduction, but it branded a broad category of transactions as "listed transactions," imposed burdensome disclosure requirements, and opened the door to an aggressive campaign challenging taxpayers who used them.

They retroactively labeled partnerships participating in the program "presumptively abusive." This aggressive IRS enforcement campaign has swept more than 1,100 syndicated conservation-easement disputes into audits and litigation, including roughly 740 cases docketed in U.S. Tax Court and about 400 transactions still under examination as of May 2026.

The IRS improperly issued Notice 2017-10, branding an entire category of these legal, decades-old transactions presumptively abusive, retroactive to 2010.

No proposed rule. No public comment. No vote by anyone accountable to voters.

Just an IRS notice — followed by an increase to a 100% audit rate for all transactions of this kind. The result was an abusive enforcement campaign that has now clogged the U.S. Tax Court with more than a thousand cases.

TENS OF MILLIONS OF TAXPAYERS MAY BE OWED IRS REFUNDS FROM COVID-ERA

If there are bad actors, of course, they should be punished. A bipartisan Senate Finance Committee investigation identified serious abuses in some syndicated conservation-easement transactions, particularly deals involving inflated land valuations and outsized deductions. But evidence that some promoters abused the deduction does not give the IRS license to presume that every transaction was fraudulent or that every investor knowingly participated in a tax shelter.

By using cookie-cutter metrics and conducting desk audits, the IRS has harassed law-abiding taxpayers, pressured them to pay tens of millions of dollars in unfair "settlement agreements," forced some to file for bankruptcy, and treated them like common criminals despite their having followed the law.

Clearly, the IRS changed tax law after the fact, which is only legal "with respect to criminal and penal cases, but not civil revenue measures." On top of that, the IRS does not make the laws. Congress does. Sadly, the IRS continued this aggressive approach during the Biden administration, when the agency received a major infusion of funding and personnel that expanded its enforcement capacity. Rather than correcting the campaign’s procedural and fairness problems, the administration allowed it to continue against taxpayers caught in these long-running conservation-easement disputes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Perhaps the most ironic part is that the IRS itself was caught engaging in illegal activity.  In a May 2026 report, the Treasury Inspector General found seven cases involving backdated penalty-approval documents; the IRS conceded more than $68 million in penalties in those cases.

Even so, IRS officials have frightening leeway to make allegations of tax fraud, then serve as judge, jury, and executioner, forcing people to pay tax bills that aren’t actually owed. It is a pattern of abuse that Americans have come to recognize: an agency substituting its own policy preferences for the law Congress wrote, then using its enforcement powers to punish law-abiding citizens who relied on the statute as written.

It’s time for Congress to amend tax laws to prohibit after-the-fact tax changes so that trust and fairness in the tax code can be restored.

In addition, the IRS should issue clear guidance on how to make a proper donation of a conservation easement and how to prudently value the deduction without creating later controversy.

Finally, the IRS should immediately end the witch hunt against law-abiding taxpayers who were encouraged by Congress and the Treasury Department for decades to participate in conservation easement programs.

Simply put, this is weaponization at its worst — and it is un-American.

item.title: MIKE SARRAILLE: Extortion 17's heroes died once. America must never let them die twice
item.description: A new Fox Nation special honors the 31 Americans killed when their CH-47 Chinook was struck in Afghanistan's Wardak Province on Aug. 6, 2011.
item.content:encoded:
PROGRAMMING ALERT: The Fox Nation special "Final Flight: The Men of Extortion 17" is available to stream now on Fox Nation.

Fifteen years after Extortion 17 became the deadliest single incident for U.S. forces in the war in Afghanistan — and the greatest loss of life in Naval Special Warfare history — our duty is to ensure the men aboard are never forgotten.

There is an old saying that a soldier dies twice: first, when he draws his final breath; and again, when his name is spoken for the last time.

On Aug. 6, 2011, some of America’s finest warriors died their first death. It is a cliché to say these men were the best of us, but in this case, it is simply true. Gen. "Wild Bill" Donovan, founder of the World War II-era Office of Strategic Services, once described such operators as "Ph.D.s who can win a bar fight" — individuals possessing brilliant, highly specialized intellects while also having the grit to get their hands dirty.

SEAL TEAM 6 MEMBER EXPLAINS BLUNT REALITY OF COMBAT AND EXPECTATIONS IN THE BLACK OPS WORLD

Thirty-one Americans, including Navy SEALs, Air Force special operators and Army aviation soldiers, alongside their Afghan commando counterparts, boarded a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to answer a call for support. The helicopter was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade in Afghanistan’s Wardak province, killing everyone aboard. In an instant, they were gone. But their stories remain.

Extortion 17 is not merely a call sign, a date or an entry in the history of a long war. It was personal. The Navy SEALs aboard that helicopter belonged to SEAL Team 6’s Gold Squadron. I knew these men. They were my brothers-in-arms.

FOREIGN BLACK OPS MEMBER REVEALS THE SECRET AMERICAN UNIT HE LOVED WORKING WITH IN COMBAT

They were among the most elite warriors our nation has ever produced — highly trained men who operated in the shadows, accepted long periods away from their families and carried burdens most Americans will never fully understand.

They were also among the kindest, most empathetic and respectful human beings you could ever meet.

That is the paradox of the American warrior.

These men possessed a rare and necessary ability. They could dim their empathy like flipping a switch, bring overwhelming violence against evil on our behalf and then return home to be dad again. They were the monsters our enemies feared and the fathers, husbands, sons and brothers their families needed.

AS AN ARMY WIDOW, I WILL NEVER FORGET HOW ORDINARY AMERICANS HONORED MY HUSBAND

On that fateful night, Rangers from the 75th Ranger Regiment were engaged with the enemy in the Tangi Valley and needed reinforcements. When the call came, the men of Extortion 17 did not hesitate.

They did not debate the danger. They did not take a vote. They simply flew off into the night.

In doing so, they upheld a covenant few Americans will ever understand: When your brothers are in harm’s way, you go. Even when the risk is extraordinary. Even when death may await you.

That is a warrior’s life.

We are blessed as a nation that such men and women still live among us — the "damn few" willing to carry the burden for the overwhelming majority.

While filming our Fox Nation special "Final Flight: The Men of Extortion 17," commemorating the 15th anniversary of their deaths, I sat down with former teammates, parents, wives and siblings of the fallen. Fifteen years have passed, but the pain remains fresh. The chairs are still empty. The voices are still missed. The holes left behind have never truly been filled.

SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW

Yet these families have moved forward — not past the loss, but with it. They carry the weight of their loved ones with the same quiet strength those warriors carried for this country. Their sacrifice did not end on Aug. 6, 2011. It continues every morning they wake up and choose to keep going.

America owes them more than a moment of silence once a year.

We owe them remembrance through action. We teach their names. We tell their stories. We teach our children that freedom is not self-sustaining. It demands strength, sacrifice, stewardship and love of country. We remind them that the peace they inherited was purchased by men and women willing to stand between their families and evil.

Remembrance is not passive. It is a duty — a duty to be worthy of their sacrifice. We cannot repay the men of Extortion 17. But we can refuse to let them die twice.
